name: Umar Nakamura

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any company, union, party or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: That's fine by me. I'll be honest, I don't usually get asked what I think about anything at work, so this makes a change.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm in the motor claims team at a car insurer's regional office, upstairs from a carpet shop on Station Road. I get in at half eight, open the queue, and work through accident reports: photos of dented bumpers, garage estimates, the little sketches people draw of the junction. I key it all into the claims system, chase the missing bits by phone, and pass the bigger ones to the handlers. I like the phone calls more than people think, because someone who's just had a crash wants a calm voice. What wears me out is the targets board, and the fact that I've been doing this six years for not much more than I started on.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Who do you work with, and who's at home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: There are eleven of us on the floor. I eat lunch with Bev, who's been there twenty years and still does everything on paper first. At home it's me and Hana, my partner, who does nights as a care worker at a home on the edge of town. Our rent went up again in September, and between us we've got maybe three weeks of money in the bank if anything goes wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly hype. Honestly, that sounds like what I've been hearing in the canteen for two years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I always say: the bosses buy a shiny system, it doesn't work, and we clean up after it. I'd post something about how the money should've gone on staff instead. In the union group chat I'd probably make a joke about the chatbot that told a customer their car was a boat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, even the routine bits are most of my job. If software reads the garage estimates and fills in the claim forms, that's half my morning gone, and they don't keep people on to watch a screen. So nothing radical for the country, maybe, but for me it could still mean fewer hours. And we're already only just paying the rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my head down and keep my numbers up, because that's what protects you there. I'd go to the union meeting in the spring and ask what the deal is if they bring in the estimate reader. And I'd stop the takeaway on Fridays and try to get our savings up to a full month. I wouldn't start using the AI stuff myself, no.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tired, mostly. It's the same feeling as when the rent letter comes. Nothing's on fire, but nothing's getting better either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why not use the AI tools yourself, if they're coming in anyway?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I don't trust them and I don't trust why they're being brought in. Bev says the minute you show them you can do your job with a robot, you've shown them they don't need you. I know that's not totally fair, but I've watched two people not get replaced already this year. I'd rather be the person who knows the claims than the person who knows the button.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned getting the savings to a full month. What would that take?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About four hundred more than we've got, which sounds like nothing until you try. Hana could pick up an extra night shift, but she's already wrecked by Thursday. So it'd be me cutting stuff: the phone contract, the gym I don't go to, the Friday curry. Getting to one month of rent saved would honestly feel like a holiday.

say: The bosses buy **shiny systems** that don't work, and the staff end up cleaning up after them.
The money spent on software should have gone on **more staff** instead.
think: Reading garage estimates and filling forms is **half my morning**, so even a small change could cut my hours.
**Fewer hours** would hit hard, because we're already only just paying the rent.
do: **Keep his numbers** up and keep his head down to stay safe on the team.
Ask at the **spring union meeting** what the deal is if the estimate reader arrives.
Cut the takeaway and phone contract to build **one month** of savings.
feel: **Tired** rather than scared, like when the rent letter arrives.
Stuck, because **nothing's getting better** even if nothing's on fire.
S0.quote: Getting to one month of rent saved would honestly feel like a holiday.
fieldNote: Even in the mildest picture, Umar sees **routine screen work** as most of his day.
His distrust of AI is about **who benefits**, not about whether it works.
Bev, his lunch colleague, shapes his view that using the tools **proves you're replaceable**.
Money is already tight with **three weeks** of savings and rising rent.

steps.text: Keep hitting the claims targets on the motor team
Ask the union in spring about the estimate-reading software
Drop the Friday takeaway, the gym and the pricey phone contract
Put the savings toward one full month of rent

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Writing, checking, answering customers. That's my whole job description you just read out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Publicly I'd say this is exactly why we need the union and proper rules. Companies shouldn't be allowed to cut a whole team and keep all the savings for shareholders. I'd share stuff about a shorter working week, because if the work gets done faster, people should get time back, not the sack.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the motor claims floor goes from eleven to maybe four within a couple of years. The ones who stay will be the handlers who deal with the messy cases and the people who are good with the computers. I'm neither. I'm average and I don't touch AI, so I'd be in the first lot to go, and I know it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push the union to get a no-redundancy deal or at least decent payouts, and I'd go to every meeting. I'd look at what Hana does, because care work is hands-on and nobody's replacing her with a chatbot. There's a care certificate course at the college on Tuesday evenings. I'd probably sign up for it, even though the idea of starting again at the bottom makes me feel sick.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like the floor's tilting. I'd still have a job for a bit, but I'd be watching every empty desk. It's the slowness that would get me, waiting to see whose name comes up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd sign up for the care course but you say you'd hate starting at the bottom. Which wins?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rent wins. I can hate it and still do it. Hana says care pays badly too, but at least the work's there and it's not going anywhere soon. If I'm going to be broke either way, I'd rather be broke in a job that exists.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on the team would you worry about most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Bev, without a doubt. She's fifty-eight and she's never going to learn a new system now, and she's the reason half our claims don't go wrong. If they let her go, she won't find another office job in this town. There's only the council and the bank, and the bank's cutting too.

say: Firms shouldn't cut whole teams and keep **all the savings** for shareholders.
If work gets done faster, people deserve a **shorter week**, not the sack.
think: The motor claims floor shrinks from **eleven to four** within a couple of years.
As an average clerk who avoids AI, he expects to be in the **first lot** to go.
do: Push the union for a **no-redundancy deal** or decent payouts.
Sign up for the **care certificate** course on Tuesday evenings at the college.
Watch Hana's line of work as a **hands-on fallback** that isn't going anywhere soon.
feel: Like the **floor's tilting**, with every empty desk a warning.
Dread at the slow wait to see **whose name** comes up.
S1.quote: If I'm going to be broke either way, I'd rather be broke in a job that exists.
fieldNote: Umar names himself as a **likely early cut**, not just someone affected.
His escape route borrows from his partner's **care work**, which feels safer because it's hands-on.
He worries more about **Bev (his colleague)** than he admits about himself.
Few local office jobs make a lost post **hard to replace**.

steps.text: Press the union for a no-redundancy deal on the claims floor
Start the Tuesday evening care certificate course at the college
Apply for care assistant shifts at Hana's care home

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That's before our lease even runs out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be angry out loud. I'd say governments let a handful of tech firms wreck millions of jobs without even asking, and I'd be at whatever protest there was. I'd tell people it's not progress if the only people who win are the ones who own the machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think I'm gone. Claims clerks are just about the first thing a thinking AI would replace, because it's all forms and rules. Maybe I'd get a few months while they move the systems over. After that, the only thing I'd have is the three years before the robots can do care work, and that's if I can even get into care.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the care course immediately, not next term. I'd ask Hana's manager about weekend shifts while I'm still at the insurer, so I've got a foot in the door. We'd cut everything back to rent, food and bills, and I'd ring my mum about whether we could move back into her spare room if the payout's small.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick, to be honest. There's no plan B that's big enough, and two years isn't long enough to make one. I'd be lying awake doing sums.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd move back to your mum's at twenty-seven. How would that be?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Humiliating, but she'd have us. Her flat's tiny, and Hana working nights would mean sleeping while my mum's got the telly on. It would be a few months of grim, and I'd tell myself it's only until the care job's steady.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the three-year gap before robots mean for you, in practical terms?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means care work is a lifeboat, but a small one with a hole in it. Everyone who loses an office job in town will be queuing for the same shifts. So I'd have to get in early and be good at it, and then hope the robots that can lift an old man safely are slower than they say.

say: Governments let a few tech firms wreck **millions of jobs** without asking anyone.
It's **not progress** if only the people who own the machines win.
think: Claims clerking is all forms and rules, so he expects to be **gone within months**.
His only room is the **three-year gap** before robots reach care work.
do: Start the **care course** immediately instead of waiting for next term.
Ask Hana's manager for **weekend shifts** while still at the insurer.
Cut spending to **rent, food and bills** and plan a move to his mum's.
feel: **Sick**, because no plan B is big enough.
Kept awake doing sums with **no time** to build anything.
S2.quote: Care work is a lifeboat, but a small one with a hole in it.
fieldNote: Umar sees **no workable plan** in two years, which drives the panic.
He clearly understands that **hands-on care** buys him about three years.
His protest instinct is real, but his private focus is **survival**.
Moving in with his mum is the **fallback** he'd hate but accept.

steps.text: Join protests against job losses from AI
Start the care certificate course this term
Cut spending to rent, food and bills only
Move into his mum's spare room if the payout is small

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is still fast. But it's not two, I'll give it that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same thing about the tech firms, but I'd add that five years is enough time to do something if governments actually tried. Retraining money, a proper safety net, a tax on the firms doing the replacing. I'd be signing every petition going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, the claims job still goes, just a bit later, maybe by 2030 when they've tested it. The difference is I could actually finish a qualification before it happens. Care work would give me until about 2034, and by then I'd be thirty-five, which feels survivable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the care certificate in the first year and then start the level above it, the one for senior carers. I'd stay at the insurer as long as they'd keep me, because it pays the rent. I'd try to save fifty a month into a separate account Hana can't see, just so we've got something when the end comes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still scared, but it's the kind of scared where you can make a list. With two years I had no list. With five, I could at least plan the next step.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: A separate account Hana can't see? Why that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because we're both terrible at leaving money alone when it's sitting there. It's not a secret, she knows about it, she just can't see the number. It's the only way I've ever saved anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take a pay cut to move into care sooner?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not straight away, no. Care pays less than claims, and right now the claims pay is all that keeps us afloat. I'd move once I'm qualified, or once they start cutting the claims floor, whichever comes first. I don't like gambling, so I'd want to see the cuts coming before I jump.

say: Five years is enough for governments to fund **retraining** and a safety net if they tried.
Firms doing the replacing should pay a **tax** to help workers move on.
think: His claims job still goes, probably **by 2030**, just later than in the fast picture.
Care work would last until **about 2034**, which feels survivable at thirty-five.
do: Finish the **care certificate** in year one, then start the senior carer level.
Stay at the insurer **as long as possible** because it pays the rent.
Save **fifty a month** in a separate account he and Hana can't easily touch.
feel: Still scared, but able to **make a list**.
Steadier, because five years gives a **next step**.
S3.quote: With two years I had no list. With five, I could at least plan the next step.
fieldNote: Umar still expects to **lose the claims job**; only the timing changes.
Extra years turn panic into **a plan** built on qualifications.
His resistance to risk shows in waiting to **see the cuts** before he jumps.
The hidden savings pot shows how **thin and fragile** their budget is.

steps.text: Sign petitions for retraining money and a tax on AI firms
Finish the care certificate and start the senior carer level
Put fifty a month into a separate savings account

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be thirty-seven. That's a whole career change, isn't it?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the version where nobody has any excuse. Ten years is long enough for unions and governments to plan who gets retrained and who pays for it. If it still goes badly, it's because someone chose that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd still lose the claims job, maybe around 2033 when they're sure of the systems. But ten years means I could become a properly senior carer, maybe even a care home deputy manager, and that work runs until robots catch up around 2039. That's a real job for a good stretch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the care certificate next year, not this year, because there's no rush. I'd work on getting a pay rise at the insurer first, through the union pay claim. Then I'd build up through the care levels over five or six years and switch when the claims floor starts thinning out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer than the others, honestly, but still uneasy in my stomach. I know how I am. With ten years I'd probably put it off for five.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd probably put it off. What would stop that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hana, most likely. She's the organised one and she'd keep asking if I'd booked the course. And watching people at work go one by one. That would get me moving faster than any plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want to happen to the insurer's office in that time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want them to retrain us properly before they cut us, and pay for it. Not a two-hour online module, a real course with time off to do it. The company will save millions, so they can afford to give eleven people a decent start somewhere else.

say: With **ten years** of warning, nobody has an excuse for workers losing out.
Unions and governments should plan **who gets retrained** and who pays.
think: He'd still lose the claims job, maybe **around 2033**.
Senior care work could carry him until robots arrive **around 2039**.
do: Back the **union pay claim** at the insurer before thinking about leaving.
Start the **care certificate** next year and build up over five or six years.
Switch to care once the **claims floor** starts thinning out.
feel: **Calmer** than in the faster pictures, but uneasy underneath.
Worried he'll **put it off**, knowing his own habits.
S4.quote: The company will save millions, so they can afford to give eleven people a decent start somewhere else.
fieldNote: Even with ten years, Umar expects his **office job to go**.
Time lets him picture a **senior care career**, not just a lifeline.
He openly admits he'd **procrastinate**, and relies on Hana (his partner) to push him.
His fairness argument centres on the **company paying** for retraining.

steps.text: Back the union pay claim at the insurer next year
Work up through the care qualifications over five or six years
Move into senior care work as the claims floor shrinks

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, no question. Two years is nothing when you've got three weeks of savings. What would help is being paid while I retrain, even half pay, so I'm not choosing between the course and the rent.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about the people who aren't good at this stuff. Everyone talks about the clever ones who'll learn to use AI. Nobody asks about the ordinary clerks who just did a decent job for years and weren't asked.

headlineQuote: Nobody asks about the ordinary clerks who just did a decent job for years and weren't asked.
portrait: Umar is a **27-year-old motor claims clerk** who keys in accident reports above a carpet shop.
He and Hana, a **night-shift care worker**, have about three weeks of savings and rising rent.
He distrusts AI as a **bosses' tool** and refuses to use it, following his colleague Bev's lead.
Across the pictures he expects to **lose the claims job** and leans on care work as a lifeboat.
More time turns his panic into a **qualification plan**, though he admits he'd put things off.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because two years is nothing with three weeks of savings.
whatWouldHelp: Being **paid while retraining**, even half pay, so the course doesn't compete with rent.
